title: From Julius Caesar to Augustus
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:53Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank point covers only Octavian's early moves in 44 BC at Year 12 depth, while the new point spans Caesar's death to Augustus becoming emperor in 27 BCE, which is a broader arc at a different depth for Year 7.

draft.title: From Julius Caesar to Augustus
card: Julius Caesar was a Roman general who won great fame and power. He became dictator, a ruler with almost total control, and many senators feared he wanted to rule like a king.
In 44 BCE a group of senators murdered Caesar. They hoped this would save the Republic, but it led to years of civil war.
Caesar's heir, his great-nephew Octavian, won that struggle for power. He took the name Augustus in 27 BCE and became Rome's first emperor.
Augustus kept the Senate and other Republican offices, but he held the real power. The rule of the Senate and elected officials had ended, and one man now ruled Rome.
draft.remember: Caesar's murder did not save the Republic. Octavian won power and became Augustus, the first emperor.

a.q: Why did some senators murder Julius Caesar in 44 BCE?
opts: They feared he wanted to rule Rome like a king
They wanted to make Octavian the first emperor
They wanted to end the Senate and rule alone
They blamed him for losing a war against Carthage
a.why: Caesar held almost total control as dictator, and some senators feared he wanted to be king. They hoped to save the Republic. The plan to make Octavian emperor is wrong, because Octavian only gained power later, after years of civil war.
a.clue: Think about what the senators hoped to protect.

b.q: Augustus kept the Senate meeting after 27 BCE. Why is he still seen as the end of the Republic?
opts: He held the real power, so one man ruled Rome
He closed the Senate and made new laws himself
He gave the Senate more power than before
He was elected as one of two consuls each year
b.why: Augustus kept Republican offices, but the real power was his, so Rome was ruled by one man. The Senate still met, so saying he closed it is wrong. A Senate that exists does not prove the Republic continued.
b.clue: Look at who held the real power, not at which buildings or offices remained.

a.best: They feared he wanted to rule Rome like a king

b.best: He held the real power, so one man ruled Rome
